Read the two numbers below before the six above. Recall on attack families that appear in the training labels is 83.0%; on families absent from them it is 62.6%. A single accuracy figure averages those together and hides the only failure mode that matters operationally. Scenario 5 is about that gap.

Layer ablation

The argument for a hybrid has to be measured against its own components, not asserted. Detection is a union of the three layers, so recall can only rise; the question is what precision it costs and which layer supplies it.

configurationprecisionrecall F1FPRaccuracyTPFPFN
signature layer only 0.9700 0.5918 0.7351 0.0242 0.7572
supervised layer only 0.9664 0.6433 0.7725 0.0296 0.7842
anomaly layer only 0.9807 0.6033 0.7470 0.0157 0.7674
signature OR anomaly 0.9662 0.6893 0.8046 0.0318 0.8094
signature OR supervised 0.9607 0.7335 0.8319 0.0396 0.8312
hybrid (deployed) 0.9599 0.7707 0.8549 0.0425 0.8511

Two honest observations from this table. The hybrid is identical to signature OR supervised, which means the anomaly layer contributes zero incremental recall on this corpus — it earns its place only by corroborating the other two for ranking, and by covering novel behaviour in principle. And the signature layer alone has an unacceptable standalone false-positive rate; it is usable here because fusion demotes uncorroborated rule hits rather than suppressing them.

Finding. The system does not stay silent, and the brief's own wording anticipates this: 413 of 9,711 benign connections raise something, a false-positive rate of 4.25% -- about 1 in 24. The layers contribute 235 rule hits, 287 supervised alerts and 152 anomaly alerts (overlapping, so these sum to more than the total). The rules doing it are R06 (vertical port scan, 113), R04 (malformed ip fragmentation, 52), R10 (guest session with file activity, 43), R11 (root shell obtained, 19), and the benign populations that trigger them are exactly the ones a real network has: a monitoring system polling many hosts, a client retrying closed ports, an anonymous FTP download, an administrator using su. No threshold on these features separates them, because at connection level they are not different -- the intent is, and intent is not in the record. What the hybrid can do is rank: 232 of these land at medium or low because no second layer corroborates them, so they sort below the corroborated attacks rather than competing with them. 173 still reach critical, which is the residual cost and is stated as such.

Finding. This is the class the feature set is best suited to, and the result says so: 2,382 of 2,421 scan connections are flagged (98.4% recall) across 6 families, 4 of them at full recall (ipsweep, nmap, portsweep, satan). Scanning is defined by the *spread* of a source's connections rather than their content, and diff_srv_rate, dst_host_diff_srv_rate and the rejected-connection rates measure that spread directly, so a hand-written rule and a learned tree arrive at nearly the same boundary. That is why recall generalises to a scanner absent from training while it collapses for unseen r2l families in scenario 5 -- the signal is geometric, not semantic. The cost of this sensitivity is scenario 1: the same rules that carry this class (R06, R07) account for 126 rule hits on benign traffic, because a monitoring sweep has the same geometry. High recall on this class and a 4.3% benign alarm rate are the same fact measured from two sides, not two independent results.

Finding. Flooding recall is 90.2% over 7,458 connections, and where it succeeds the reason is mechanical rather than statistical: a half-open flood pins serror_rate near 1 and drives count into the hundreds, which no benign profile in the corpus reaches. The cost is the queue. DoS traffic produces 6,731 of the 10,303 alerts in this run -- 65% of everything an analyst would see -- across only 169 distinct alert signatures. Per-flow alerting is the wrong granularity for a flood: correlation into one incident per (rule, service, state) collapses it by a factor of 40. The recall that is missing is concentrated in specific families -- mailbomb 1.4% of 293, processtable 37.5% of 685 -- not spread evenly across the class.

Finding. This is where the hybrid architecture earns its cost, and also where the system is weakest overall. R2L recall is 25.5% and U2R 59.7% across 21 families, and the aggregate hides which layer is doing the work. These are the rarest classes in the corpus, so the supervised layer has the least to learn from: it recovers guess_passwd 0.0%, sendmail 0.0%, snmpgetattack 0.0%. The signature layer does not care about class balance -- R09 counts failed logins, R10 flags guest sessions that create files, and R11/R12 look for root_shell, su_attempted and root-level file activity -- so on 9 of these families it is the strongest layer of the three. The largest hybrid-over-supervised gains are loadmodule +100%, sqlattack +100%, buffer_overflow +60%. The anomaly layer contributes little here (its best family here is httptunnel at 32.3%), because a brute-force login and a root shell are statistically ordinary connections; where it is 0.000 that is a null result and it is reported as one. Two honest caveats remain. First, this is not detection of the attack but of its aftermath -- a matched R11 means a root shell was already obtained. Second, the same counters fire on an administrator legitimately using su, which is part of the scenario-1 false-positive rate: the signature layer trades false alarms on benign admin activity for recall on privilege escalation. On this corpus that trade is worth making, but it is a trade, not a free improvement.

Finding. Recall on attack families present in the training labels is 83.0%; on families absent from them it is 62.6%. That gap of 20% is the single most important number in this evaluation, and it is the one a headline accuracy figure hides. The worst case is 'snmpguess' (r2l, 331 connections): hybrid recall 0.0%, with the signature layer at 0.0%, the supervised layer at 0.0% and the anomaly layer at 0.0%. Every layer fails for its own reason and the reasons compound rather than cancel: no rule was written for behaviour nobody had characterised, the classifier has no decision region for a class it never saw, and the anomaly layer -- the one layer that is supposed to cover exactly this -- is silent because these connections are not statistically unusual. They are ordinary-looking sessions on ordinary services carrying a hostile payload. At connection-record granularity they are genuinely indistinguishable from benign traffic, so this is not a tuning problem: no threshold on these features separates them. Closing it needs different evidence -- payload inspection, or host-level telemetry -- not a better model over the same features.

Finding. The pipeline runs unchanged on flows assembled from raw packets, which is the useful part: the same rules and the same fitted models apply to 755 flows reconstructed from the capture in 2.02s. What the capture shows is the limit of the record format rather than of the detector. No alert at all is raised for 10.0.0.50 (0/90 flows, top severity none). Rule-backed detections: 10.0.0.66 (30/30 flows, top severity critical) via R07 x27, R06 x23; 10.0.0.99 (595/595 flows, top severity critical) via R01 x495. Flagged by the learned layers with no rule behind them: 10.0.0.77 (40/40 flows, top severity low). Those are the interesting ones. They are detected, but they are detected weakly -- no signature matched, so nothing corroborates the models and the corroboration discount pushes them to the bottom of the queue. The structural reason is the record format: the dst_host_* features summarise behaviour per destination, and a sweep touches each destination once, so that history is empty at the moment each flow is scored. A scan that spreads across hosts defeats features that summarise behaviour per host, and the flow-level rules that would catch it have nothing to count. That is an argument for correlating across destinations at a level above the flow record, which this design does not do.

Concrete true positives, false positives and false negatives

Most isolating features: conn_per_second=510 (+9.0 SD from the benign mean); dst_host_srv_count=9 (-2.0 SD from the benign mean); dst_host_diff_srv_rate=0.97 (+7.2 SD from the benign mean). Corroboration: 3 of 3 layers agree (signature, supervised, anomaly).

Feature groups and why each was selected

Requirement B asks for justification, not a list. Each group below exists because a specific attack behaviour is only visible through it.

volume

Byte and packet volumes separate bulk transfers and amplification floods from interactive sessions.

src_bytesdst_bytesdurationbyte_ratiobytes_per_secondlog_src_byteslog_dst_bytes

connection_rate

Counts of connections to the same host/service in the trailing 2-second window are the primary signal for scanning and flooding.

countsrv_countdst_host_countdst_host_srv_countconn_per_second

error_behaviour

SYN-error and rejection rates spike when a scanner touches closed ports or a SYN flood exhausts the backlog.

serror_ratesrv_serror_ratererror_ratesrv_rerror_ratedst_host_serror_ratedst_host_srv_serror_ratedst_host_rerror_ratedst_host_srv_rerror_rateerror_pressure

service_spread

A host contacted across many different services with little repeat is horizontal scanning; a single service repeated is a flood.

same_srv_ratediff_srv_ratesrv_diff_host_ratedst_host_same_srv_ratedst_host_diff_srv_ratedst_host_same_src_port_ratedst_host_srv_diff_host_rateservice_entropy_proxy

authentication

Failed logins, guest logins and shell/root activity are the only content-level evidence of brute force and privilege escalation.

num_failed_loginslogged_inis_guest_loginis_host_loginroot_shellsu_attemptednum_roothotnum_compromisednum_file_creationsnum_shellsnum_access_filesauth_pressure

protocol

Protocol, service and TCP flag state give the categorical context that makes the numeric features interpretable.

Throughput and the cost of inline detection

Section 5 of the brief asks what running this inline would cost. These figures come from the same run that produced the metrics above, on this machine, single-threaded, in pure NumPy with no compiled extensions.

Throughput

Per stage

stageseconds
signature_s0.0754
supervised_s2.3599
anomaly_s24.5246
total_s26.9599
rows_per_second836.2050

Per-alert explanations use exact tree traversal in Python and are computed on alerted rows only; the throughput above excludes them. The anomaly layer dominates, which is the expected shape: isolation-forest scoring walks every tree for every row and is not vectorised across trees here. A production deployment would evaluate the cheap signature layer inline and the two model layers out-of-band on a mirrored feed, which keeps the forwarding path at the signature layer's cost.
